content: Sickle cell disease is a genetic condition characterized by a defect in red blood cells caused by the presence of abnormal hemoglobin, known as sickled hemoglobin. The primary treatment strategies for this condition include preventive and supportive measures. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a therapeutic approach aimed at replacing the defective blood-forming stem cells and their progenitors to correct the underlying disorder. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can improve survival rates and prevent the symptoms and complications associated with sickle cell disease. Additionally, the review sought to assess the risks of this procedure in comparison to its potential long-term benefits for individuals with the disease. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register. This register is compiled from electronic searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and quarterly searches of MEDLINE. Trial registries were also searched for ongoing studies, with the most recent search of the Haemoglobinopathies Trials Register completed on December 9, 2019. The search for ongoing trials extended up to April 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials that compared any method of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with either other transplantation methods or standard preventive and supportive interventions. These interventions included periodic blood transfusions, hydroxyurea therapy, antibiotics, pain management, and supplemental oxygen. The inclusion criteria were broad, encompassing individuals with any type of sickle cell disease, regardless of gender or clinical setting. However, no trials met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in this review. Of the 12 potentially eligible trials identified, 11 were excluded, and the remaining trial is an ongoing study that may be considered for inclusion in a future update of the review. The authors concluded that current evidence on the use of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to improve survival and prevent symptoms and complications in sickle cell disease is limited to observational studies and other less rigorous forms of research. No eligible randomized controlled trials were identified to assess the benefits or risks of this intervention. Nevertheless, there is an ongoing quasi-randomized trial comparing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation with standard care. This highlights the need for a well-designed, multicenter randomized controlled trial to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, taking into account the sickle cell status and disease severity in affected individuals.
